title: "Judge response theory for the consensual assessment of creativity in football: Judge leniency, discrimination, and the number of judges"
shorttitle: "Judge response theory for creativity ratings in football"
author:

abstract: |
  The Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) is the standard procedure for rating the creativity of products. The reliability of CAT scores depends on how many judges are aggregated and on how these judges differ, and the evidence on both questions is domain-specific; for actions in sport, no such evidence exists. The aim of this study was to model judge leniency and judge discrimination and to quantify score reliability as a function of the number of judges, using Judge Response Theory (JRT) on CAT ratings of football actions. Twenty-two raters provided 7,844 ratings of 3,669 football actions on a 7-point scale in a sparse but connected rating design. The ratings were analysed with a Bayesian graded-response JRT model with rater-specific leniency and discrimination and shared thresholds. This model was compared with a nested equal-discrimination model by Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO), and an item response theory decision study (D-study) projected reliability for different numbers of judges per action. Posterior-mean rater discrimination ranged from 0.96 to 3.24. The rater-specific model had a higher expected log predictive density than the equal-discrimination model (difference = 163.25, *SE* = 19.68). The empirical reliability of the JRT scores was .66. Marginal reliability was .51 for one judge per action, .65 at the realised 1.73 judges per action, .81 for four judges, and .91 for ten judges. These results suggest that judges of football actions are not interchangeable, that fair scores should model judges rather than average them, and that panels of about two judges per action give only modest precision for individual actions [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

# Introduction

Creativity is widely regarded as one of the key competencies of the modern world. Employers rank creative thinking among the core skills of the workforce and expect its importance to grow [@worldeconomicforum2025] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM: check wording against the report], and the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) assessed creative thinking as an innovative domain in its 2022 cycle [@oecd2024]. In sport, creativity is considered one of the key qualities to be developed and evaluated in players [@safardilha2019; @santos2016] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM: check the safardilha2019 claim against the source]. The assessment of creativity is therefore a fundamental task, both in society in general and in sport in particular.

Creativity research commonly distinguishes four facets of creativity: the creative person, the creative process, the creative product, and the press, that is, the environment in which creativity occurs [@batey2012]. Each of these facets requires its own measurement approach [@barbot2019; @barbot2019b]. The present paper is concerned with the product facet, namely creative actions performed in football matches, and with the evaluation of these products by others.

The Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) is the established method for evaluating creative products [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011; @kaufman2024]. In the CAT, judges who are familiar with the domain rate products independently and relative to one another, without being given an imposed definition of creativity [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. Although the procedure rests on subjective judgements, it typically yields reasonable agreement: when independent domain experts rate products, coefficient alphas usually exceed .70 [@baer2004; @kaufman2008; @hennessey2011]. Considerably lower agreement has also been reported, however, and has been attributed to differences between judges in rating procedure, in their use of the rating scale, and in their beliefs about creativity [@long2015; @cseh2019]. The CAT has nevertheless produced important insights into the genesis of creative products, most prominently the intrinsic-motivation principle of creativity [@amabile1985; @hennessey2010].

The reliability of CAT scores rests on aggregation across judges. As already noted by @amabile1982, the Spearman–Brown reliability of an aggregated rating depends jointly on the mean inter-judge correlation and on the number of judges, so that a larger panel compensates for lower agreement between individual judges. Conversely, a high alpha obtained from a large panel can mask low agreement among individual judges [@kaufman2008]. A rule of thumb of five to ten judges is often cited [@kaufman2008a]. @cseh2019, however, argue that the appropriate number of judges depends on the nature of the creative product and on the domain in which it is produced, that it therefore cannot be set in general, and that each research domain requires empirical evidence on the necessary number of judges and on their required expertise. Generalizability theory formalises the same question for classical scores in the form of decision studies [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM whether to mention G-theory].

In sport, research on creativity has focused mainly on the creative process, for example on divergent thinking [@memmert2011]. Creative products, that is, the actions themselves, have received less attention. Expert ratings of actions in competition have been obtained successfully and showed face validity by predicting the temporal proximity of actions to goals [@kempe2018]; these ratings were provided by trained experts using a scale that originated in research on tactical creativity [@memmert2007]. Expert judgements of on-field actions have also been used in further studies of creativity in football [@zahno2023; @zahno2024; @dejoode2023]. These studies, however, report agreement indices at most, and none of them provides the parameters needed to design a CAT study of football actions, such as the number of judges or the expertise they require.

Sport research therefore needs an empirical reference for the design of CAT studies of actions. A key aspect of such a design is how ratings from different judges are combined into "fair" scores that properly reflect rater tendencies [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM: this bridging paragraph replaces the brief's aim paragraph, whose formal aim is moved to the end of the Introduction].

The methodological framework that is arguably most relevant to this question is item response theory (IRT) [@lord1980; @embretson2013; @myszkowski2019]. IRT models the probability of each observed response as a function of a latent attribute of the person or product and of parameters that characterise the item, typically its location and its discrimination [@embretson2013; @deayala2022]. In contrast to classical test theory, in which the observed score is decomposed by definition into a true score and an error component, IRT specifies a falsifiable measurement model, places persons and items on a common latent scale, and quantifies measurement precision conditionally on the level of the latent attribute rather than as a single sample-level coefficient [@myszkowski2019]. For ordinal rating scales, polytomous models such as the graded response model [@samejima1969] and the generalized partial credit model [@muraki1992] estimate a discrimination parameter and a set of category thresholds for each item.

Rasch models [@rasch1960] are a special case of IRT in which all items are constrained to discriminate equally. This constraint makes the raw score a sufficient statistic for the latent attribute and yields specific objectivity [@bond2020]. Their polytomous extensions, the rating scale model [@andrich1978] and the partial credit model [@masters1982], differ in whether all items share one set of category thresholds or each item has its own. Rasch models have been adapted to ratings by judges in the form of the many-facet Rasch model (MFRM), which adds rater severity as an additive facet; so-called fair averages then express ratee measures on the original rating metric as if every ratee had been judged by a rater of average severity [@linacre1989; @eckes2015]. Beyond severity, MFRM diagnostics have been used to detect further rater effects such as central tendency, restriction of range, randomness, and halo [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. In creativity research, @primi2019 showed that raters differed in severity, that these differences confound scores whenever different raters score different subsets of responses, and that MFRM-adjusted scores were robust under moderate amounts of planned missing data. In judged sports, the MFRM has been used to monitor judges of performance quality, though not of creativity [@looney2004; @anderlucci2021].

The development from classical scoring to Judge Response Theory (JRT) can be described as a successive relaxation of assumptions about judges. Sum or mean scores, still the default in CAT research, treat judges as interchangeable, (essentially) τ-equivalent measures of the same attribute [@myszkowski2019]; such scores are comparable across products only if all products are rated by the same judges or by equally severe judges [@primi2019]. The MFRM models severity additively but retains the defining constraint of the Rasch family, namely equal discrimination; differences in discrimination have no parameter in this model and surface only indirectly as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021], and interactions between raters and the rating scale were left to future research by @primi2019. For the CAT, the assumption of equally accurate judges is questionable, because panels are often heterogeneous in expertise, prior training, attention, and understanding of the instructions, and because judges may prefer central or extreme categories [@myszkowski2021]. JRT addresses these limitations by transposing the IRT framework to multiple-judge situations: judges are treated as items whose severity, discrimination, and category thresholds can be estimated individually, for instance with the graded response model or the generalized partial credit model [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. Constraints such as equal discrimination thereby become testable by comparing nested models rather than being imposed a priori, and JRT yields fair scores for the rated products together with product-specific standard errors, as well as an explicit model of judge behaviour [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. JRT has been applied in recent creativity research [@barbot2023; @pellegrino2025], and simulation-based work has addressed the planning of missing-data rating designs [@forthmann2023].

However, to our knowledge, no study has modelled CAT ratings of sport actions with IRT or JRT [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM novelty claim; consider a SPORTDiscus/PsycINFO search]. The closest precedents are Rasch-family analyses of judges of performance quality [@looney2004; @anderlucci2021], a non-IRT evaluation of judge accuracy in gymnastics [@heiniger2021], a Rasch validation of a coach-completed creativity-related questionnaire that rates players rather than actions [@shin2025], and CAT-like ratings of football actions that report agreement indices only [@kempe2018; @zahno2023]. Consequently, it is unknown for football actions whether judges discriminate equally, how much they differ in leniency, and how many judges per action are needed for reliable scores, which is precisely the domain-specific evidence called for by @cseh2019.

The aim of the present study was to model judge leniency and judge discrimination in a large set of CAT ratings of football actions with JRT, and to quantify how reliable the resulting scores are as a function of the number of judges. Two research questions (RQs) guided the study:

- **RQ1. Judge behaviour.** How do judges differ in leniency and discrimination, and is the equal-discrimination constraint tenable? This question includes the use of the rating categories. The comparison of the rater-specific model with the equal-discrimination model was exploratory [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM: was the equal-discrimination comparison planned a priori or exploratory? Was anything preregistered?].
- **RQ2. Reliability and panel size.** How reliable are the JRT scores at the realised panel size, and how does reliability depend on the number of judges per action?

To answer these questions, we fitted a Bayesian graded-response JRT model, compared it with the nested equal-discrimination model by Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO), and conducted an IRT decision study (D-study). The study is intended as a design reference for CAT studies in sport. Rater expertise, choices concerning the rating scale, and comparisons of scoring approaches are beyond the scope of this paper.

# Methods

## Study overview and design

This was a CAT-style rating study in which independent raters judged the creativity of football actions taken from real matches [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. ## Data preprocessing

The raw export contained 9,150 rows and 23 pseudonymised rater identifiers. Five cleaning steps were applied in sequence (Appendix A, @tbl-cleaning-log). First, rows in which the rater had chosen the "action not recognised" option were removed (1,292 rows); this was the largest exclusion. Second, rows with missing action or rater identifiers were to be removed (0 rows). Third, ratings outside the set {1, ..., 7} were removed (1 row, a rating of 0). Fourth, rows with missing ratings were to be removed (0 rows). Fifth, duplicate rater–action pairs were resolved by keeping the last entry: 25 duplicated rows formed 11 pairs and 1 triple, so that 13 rows were removed; in one of these pairs the two ratings differed. The final sample comprised 7,844 ratings of 3,669 actions by 22 raters.

Two aspects of the preprocessing require comment. First, although the raw export contained 23 rater identifiers, the cleaned data contain 22 raters. ## Realised rating design and descriptive agreement

The 7,844 ratings were distributed sparsely across actions and raters (@tbl-overview-ratings-per-action). On average, an action received 2.14 ratings, and the harmonic mean number of ratings per action was 1.73. Of the 3,669 actions, 898 (24.5%) received one rating, 2,080 (56.7%) received two ratings, and 691 (18.8%) received three or more ratings, with a maximum of 12. The number of ratings per rater ranged from 2 to 1,174, with a median of 316.5. The degree distributions of the design are shown in Appendix B (@fig-overview-degree-distributions).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/01_data_overview.ipynb#tbl-overview-ratings-per-action >}}

The rater–action graph formed a single connected component that contained all actions and all raters, so that all raters and actions can be placed on one common scale and no data had to be excluded for connectivity. The overlap of each rater with their best-connected partner varied widely, however (Appendix B, @fig-overview-rater-overlap). Three raters shared fewer than 15 actions with their best-connected partner (R22, R21, and R20). These three raters also contributed very few ratings (R22: 2; R21: 9; R20: 13) and therefore carry little information about their own rater parameters.

The allocation of actions to raters was not balanced with respect to action type. A chi-square test of the rater × StatsBomb action type table gave $\chi^2$(210) = 1260.2, *p* < .001, Cramér's *V* = .127. The share of passes, for example, ranged from 46.5% (R13) to 77.8% (R21) of a rater's actions. Because 49% of the cells had expected counts below 5, this chi-square approximation is rough and serves descriptive purposes only.

For comparability with common CAT reporting, we also computed Krippendorff's α at the interval level on the incomplete rater × action matrix. Krippendorff's α was .42, based on the 2,771 actions (75.5%) with at least two ratings. We report this coefficient only as a crude agreement index that treats raters as interchangeable. It is not a reliability of the JRT scores, and no confidence interval is available for it. Moreover, the interval level treats the ordinal rating categories as equally spaced [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM whether to note this].

## Judge response theory model

The ratings were modelled with a graded-response formulation [@samejima1969] within the JRT framework [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. For rating $Y_{ij}$ of action $i$ by rater $j$,

$$
\eta_{ij} = a_j \theta_i + \lambda_j, \qquad
\Pr(Y_{ij} \le k) = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\tau_k - \eta_{ij}\right), \quad k = 1, \ldots, 6,
$$

where $\theta_i$ is the creativity of action $i$, $a_j$ is the discrimination of rater $j$, $\lambda_j$ is the leniency of rater $j$, and $\tau_1 < \cdots < \tau_6$ are six ordered cutpoints shared by all raters (an ordered-logistic likelihood). Leniency is defined relative to the average rater through a sum-to-zero constraint, and higher values indicate a more lenient rater. Compared with the general JRT graded response model, in which each judge has individual thresholds $b_{jk}$ [@myszkowski2021], the present model is constrained to shared thresholds plus a rater-specific location shift. Rater-specific thresholds were not estimated, so a common category structure across raters was assumed, not tested.

The scale was identified by $\theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. Leniency followed $\boldsymbol{\lambda} \sim \text{ZeroSumNormal}(\sigma_\lambda)$ with $\sigma_\lambda \sim \text{Exponential}(1)$. Discrimination was parameterised on the log scale in non-centred form, $\log a_j = \mu_{\log a} + z_j \, \sigma_{\log a}$, with $z_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $\mu_{\log a} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, and $\sigma_{\log a} \sim \text{Exponential}(2)$. The cutpoints followed $\boldsymbol{\tau} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}, 1.5)$ with an ordered transform, where $\mathbf{m}$ contains six equally spaced values from −2.5 to 2.5. [**FILL IN:** rationale for the prior choices (e.g., weakly informative on the logit scale)]{.mark} [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM whether to include]

To examine the equal-discrimination constraint (RQ1), we fitted a nested model in which $\log a_j = \mu_{\log a}$ for all raters, so that $\sigma_{\log a}$ is absent; all other parts of the model were identical. This model corresponds to judges discriminating equally, as Rasch-family models assume. It is a constraint within JRT, not a rival scoring approach.

The posterior mean of $\theta_i$ served as the score of action $i$, its posterior standard deviation (*PSD*) as the standard error, and the 2.5th and 97.5th posterior percentiles as its 95% credible interval.

## Estimation and model checking

Both models were estimated in PyMC [@abrilpla2023] with the No-U-Turn Sampler [@hoffman2014], using 4 chains of 2,000 draws each after 2,000 tuning steps, a target acceptance rate of 0.95, jitter+adapt_diag initialisation, and the random seed 20260713. Convergence was judged by the criteria stated in the analysis notebook: rank-normalised split $\hat{R}$ < 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes (ESS) > 400, and no divergent transitions [@vehtari2021]. Diagnostics were computed with ArviZ [@kumar2019a].

Model fit was assessed with a posterior predictive check in which the observed share of each rating category and the observed mean rating of each rater were compared with their 95% posterior predictive intervals. Replicated data sets were drawn from every 10th posterior draw. [**FILL IN:** number of posterior predictive replicate data sets (not printed by the notebook)]{.mark}

Two interval conventions are used. Rater parameters, posterior predictive checks, and action scores are summarised by 95% intervals (2.5th to 97.5th percentiles). Thresholds and hyperparameters are summarised by 89% equal-tailed intervals (ETIs), as in the exported posterior summary. No prior predictive checks or prior-sensitivity analyses were conducted.

## Model comparison, information, and reliability

The rater-specific and the equal-discrimination models were compared by their expected log pointwise predictive density (elpd), estimated with PSIS-LOO [@vehtari2017]. The standard error of the elpd difference was computed from the pointwise differences $d_n$ as $\sqrt{N \cdot \operatorname{Var}(d_n)}$. [**FILL IN:** decision criterion used to judge the elpd difference (e.g., difference relative to its SE) and whether it was specified before the analysis]{.mark} Pareto-$k$ values above 0.7 flag observations for which the importance-sampling approximation is unreliable [@vehtari2017]; we report the share of such observations for each model. This comparison was exploratory [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM a priori vs. exploratory].

To describe where on the latent continuum each rater is informative, the graded-response Fisher information of each rater was computed by plugging the posterior means of $a_j$, $\lambda_j$, and $\tau_k$ into the information function, on a grid of $\theta$ from −4 to 4 in steps of 0.02. The mean information per rating across the rater pool was defined in the same way, as the average over the 22 raters. These are plug-in values that carry no posterior uncertainty.

To address RQ2, two reliability coefficients were computed. The empirical reliability of the JRT scores was defined as

$$
\rho_{\text{emp}} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta})}{\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}) + \overline{\mathit{PSD}^2}},
$$

where $\hat{\theta}$ denotes the posterior-mean scores and $\overline{\mathit{PSD}^2}$ the mean squared posterior standard deviation across actions. The marginal reliability for $k$ judges per action was defined as

$$
\rho(k) = \left[ 1 + \int \phi(\theta) \left[ k \, \bar{I}(\theta) \right]^{-1} d\theta \right]^{-1},
$$

where $\phi$ is the standard normal density and $\bar{I}(\theta)$ is the mean plug-in information per rating across the 22 raters [@green1984]. In an IRT D-study, $\rho(k)$ was evaluated for $k = 1, \ldots, 10$ and at the realised harmonic-mean number of ratings per action. This D-study is the IRT analogue of the Spearman–Brown projection of the classical CAT literature [@amabile1982]. It assumes that judges are drawn at random from the pool with equal weights; it neither weights raters by their actual rating volume nor provides uncertainty for the projected values.

The JRT analysis was run in Python 3.12.3 with numpy 2.4.6, pandas 3.0.3, scipy 1.18.0, matplotlib 3.11.0, networkx 3.6.1, pymc 6.1.0, and arviz 1.2.0. Data preprocessing and descriptive analyses were run in a Python 3.12.9 kernel. # Results

## Overview and model estimation

As outlined in the Introduction, our aim was to model judge leniency and judge discrimination in CAT ratings of football actions with JRT and to quantify the reliability of the resulting scores as a function of the number of judges. This section first reports model estimation and fit, then the results for RQ1 (category use, leniency, discrimination, the equal-discrimination comparison, and rater information), and finally the results for RQ2 (reliability, score precision, and the D-study).

The rater-specific model showed no divergent transitions. The largest split $\hat{R}$ across all parameters was 1.0048, the smallest bulk ESS was 2,014, and the smallest tail ESS was 3,034 (both for the hyperparameters). Every parameter group therefore met the stated criteria, and no convergence warnings were logged (Appendix C, @tbl-jrt-convergence and @fig-jrt-traceplots). The equal-discrimination model likewise showed no divergent transitions, with a largest $\hat{R}$ of 1.0038 and a smallest ESS of 1,552 (Appendix C). In the posterior predictive check, all 7 of 7 observed category shares and all 22 of 22 observed rater means fell inside their 95% posterior predictive intervals (Appendix D, @fig-jrt-ppc). This check covers only the pooled category shares and the rater means; per-rater category distributions and action-level checks were not examined.

## RQ1: Judge behaviour

### Category use

As can be seen in @fig-overview-rating-distribution, ratings were concentrated in the lower part of the scale. Categories 1 and 2 together accounted for 52.9% of all ratings, whereas categories 6 and 7 together accounted for 5.7%. Category 2 was the most frequent category (2,116 ratings) and category 7 the least frequent (109 ratings); from category 2 upward, frequency fell with each higher category.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/01_data_overview.ipynb#fig-overview-rating-distribution >}}

The posterior means of the six shared cutpoints rose from −2.25 to 6.44 (89% ETIs in Appendix E, @tbl-jrt-model-summary). The gaps between consecutive cutpoints were 2.05, 1.43, 1.35, 1.67, and 2.19 (@tbl-jrt-derived-counts). The smallest gap thus lay between the third and fourth cutpoints, and the largest between the fifth and sixth cutpoints. Because these thresholds are shared by all raters, individual differences in scale use enter the model only through leniency (see Judge response theory model).

### Descriptive rater response styles

Before modelling, raters already differed visibly in how they used the scale (@fig-overview-rater-response-styles). Raw rater means ranged from 1.76 (R06) to 3.84 (R18). R06 had the highest floor rate (.58), and five raters had a ceiling rate of zero. The descriptive statistics of R22, R21, and R20 rest on very few ratings and should be read with caution.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/01_data_overview.ipynb#fig-overview-rater-response-styles >}}

### Leniency

The posterior leniency estimates are shown in panel B of @fig-jrt-rater-parameters; the full rater table is given in Appendix E (@tbl-jrt-rater-parameters). Posterior-mean leniency ranged from −2.93 (R06) to 1.63 (R18), and the between-rater standard deviation of leniency was $\sigma_\lambda$ = 1.23 (89% ETI [0.96, 1.58]). For 16 of the 22 raters, the 95% credible interval of leniency excluded zero: 8 raters were more lenient and 8 less lenient than the average rater (@tbl-jrt-derived-counts). The raters with the lowest and the highest leniency (R06 and R18) were also the raters with the lowest and the highest raw means. The leniency intervals of R20, R21, and R22 included zero. Note that $\lambda_j$ expresses leniency relative to the average rater, not relative to an absolute zero point.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02d_judge_response_theory.ipynb#fig-jrt-rater-parameters >}}

### Discrimination

Raters also differed in discrimination (@fig-jrt-rater-parameters, panel A). Posterior-mean discrimination had a median of 2.08 and ranged from 0.96 (R18) to 3.24 (R02), a max/min ratio of 3.39 (@tbl-jrt-derived-counts). No rater had a posterior-mean discrimination below 0.5. The pool discrimination $\exp(\mu_{\log a})$ (posterior median) was 1.87, with $\mu_{\log a}$ = 0.62 (89% ETI [0.47, 0.77]) and $\sigma_{\log a}$ = 0.39 (89% ETI [0.28, 0.52]; @tbl-jrt-model-summary). For 11 of the 22 raters, the 95% credible interval of the deviation of their log discrimination from the pool mean ($\log a_j - \mu_{\log a}$) excluded zero: 6 raters lay above and 5 below the pool.

The figure shows the marginal 95% intervals of $a_j$ against the point value of the pool discrimination (dashed line). A count read from the figure can therefore differ from the count reported above: R07, R08, and R14 have marginal lower bounds above the dashed line, but their deviation intervals include zero, so they are not counted as lying above the pool. The lower bound of R09's deviation interval (0.0012) lay close to zero [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM whether to mention]. The posterior SDs of $a_j$ were largest for the raters with the fewest ratings (R22: 0.68, *n* = 2; R20: 0.58, *n* = 13; R21: 0.50, *n* = 9), whose discrimination is therefore poorly determined.

### Equal-discrimination comparison

The PSIS-LOO comparison of the two models is summarised in @tbl-jrt-equal-discrimination-loo. The rater-specific model had the higher elpd (−11,537.93 vs. −11,701.19 for the equal-discrimination model), with an elpd difference of 163.25 (*SE* = 19.68); the analysis notebook reports the ratio of the difference to its standard error as 8.3. The effective numbers of parameters ($p_\text{loo}$) were 2,573.69 for the rater-specific model and 2,375.88 for the equal-discrimination model.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02d_judge_response_theory.ipynb#tbl-jrt-equal-discrimination-loo >}}

For both models, ArviZ warned that the estimated Pareto-$k$ exceeded 0.7 for some observations. The share of observations with $k$ > 0.7 was 2.80% for the rater-specific model and 0.14% for the equal-discrimination model. No further Pareto-$k$ details (count, maximum, or share above 1) are available, and no re-check of the affected observations was conducted.

### Rater information

@fig-jrt-category-curves-information illustrates the category probabilities and information functions of the raters with the lowest, median, and highest discrimination. Peak information per rater ranged from 0.29 (R18) to 3.28 (R02). The mean information per rating across the pool peaked at 1.33, at $\theta$ = 0.74, that is, above the average action. Raters with lower leniency tended to have their information peak at higher values of $\theta$ (e.g., R06 peaked at $\theta$ = 1.74 and R01 at $\theta$ = 2.10). These information values are plug-in estimates without uncertainty, resolved on a grid with a step of 0.02.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02d_judge_response_theory.ipynb#fig-jrt-category-curves-information >}}

## RQ2: Reliability and number of judges

### Reliability at the realised panel size

The empirical reliability of the JRT scores was .66. The marginal reliability at the realised harmonic-mean number of 1.73 ratings per action was .65; the two coefficients are different quantities. No interval is available for either coefficient. Across the 3,669 actions, the posterior-mean scores had an SD of 0.813 and ranged from −2.08 to 3.08.

### Precision by number of ratings

Score precision depended on the number of ratings an action received (@tbl-jrt-score-precision). The mean posterior SD of $\theta$ fell from 0.65 for actions with one rating (898 actions) to 0.40 for actions with five or more ratings (211 actions), and the mean width of the 95% credible interval fell from 2.58 to 1.57. Both quantities decreased monotonically with the number of ratings. The ranges overlapped heavily between groups, however; for example, the largest posterior SD among actions with two ratings (0.86) exceeded the smallest posterior SD among actions with one rating (0.46).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02d_judge_response_theory.ipynb#tbl-jrt-score-precision >}}

### D-study

The results of the D-study are shown in panel B of @fig-jrt-information-reliability and in @tbl-jrt-d-study; panel A shows the information of the rater pool, of which only the mean information per rating is reported in the text. Marginal reliability rose from .51 for one judge per action to .91 for ten judges, and the largest one-step increase occurred from one to two judges (.68 at $k$ = 2). The tabled values first exceeded .70 at $k$ = 3 (.76), reached .80 or more from $k$ = 4 (.81), and reached .90 or more from $k$ = 9 (.90) [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM use of .70/.80/.90 benchmarks]. These values are model-based projections under the assumption of randomly drawn judges and carry no uncertainty bands.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02d_judge_response_theory.ipynb#fig-jrt-information-reliability >}}

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02d_judge_response_theory.ipynb#tbl-jrt-d-study >}}

Taken together, the results indicated that raters in this dataset differed in leniency and discrimination, and that action-level precision at the realised panel size was limited [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

# Discussion

This study set out to model judge leniency and judge discrimination in CAT ratings of football actions with JRT and to quantify the reliability of the resulting scores as a function of the number of judges. Regarding RQ1, raters differed in both leniency and discrimination, and the model with rater-specific discrimination had a higher estimated out-of-sample predictive accuracy than the model in which all raters discriminate equally. Regarding RQ2, the reliability of the JRT scores at about two judges per action was modest, and the D-study showed how marginal reliability rises as judges are added [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

## Judges are not interchangeable

The differences in discrimination are consistent with JRT applications in other creativity tasks, which have likewise reported that judges differ in discrimination [@myszkowski2021; @barbot2023; @pellegrino2025] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. They are also in line with the attribution of low CAT agreement to differences between raters in procedure, scale use, and beliefs about creativity [@long2015] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. The present results extend the finding of @primi2019 that raters differ in severity: in our data, raters differed not only in their location on the scale but also in how sharply their ratings separated more from less creative actions, a property for which the MFRM has no parameter [@myford2004] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. In judged sports, judge quality has similarly been treated as a property of individual judges in Rasch-based and statistical monitoring systems [@looney2004; @anderlucci2021; @heiniger2021]; the present study transfers this perspective to creativity ratings, with discrimination as an explicit judge parameter [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

## Consequences for mean and Rasch-family scoring

Mean scores and Rasch-family fair averages weight all judges equally with respect to discrimination [@myszkowski2019; @primi2019]. Because the equal-discrimination constraint predicted the present ratings less well than rater-specific discrimination, these scoring approaches rest on an assumption that the present data did not support [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. We emphasise that this is an argument from the literature combined with our model comparison: no scoring methods were compared directly in this study, so the practical size of the resulting differences in action scores remains to be established [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

## Panel size

The D-study speaks directly to the call of @cseh2019 for domain-specific evidence on the number of judges. In the present pool, a marginal reliability of .80 was first reached with four judges per action, which lies just below the lower end of the five-to-ten-judge rule of thumb [@kaufman2008a] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. At the realised panel size of about two judges per action, however, the empirical reliability of .66 fell below the conventional .70 benchmark for expert CAT panels [@baer2004; @kaufman2008], although coefficients from different frameworks are not directly comparable [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. @kempe2018 reported agreement for a panel of three trained experts, a design that differs from the present sparse panel of heterogeneous raters, so that neither the designs nor the reported coefficients map onto each other directly [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. Krippendorff's α, finally, is a crude agreement index that treats raters as interchangeable; it is a different quantity from the model-based reliabilities and should not be compared with them in size [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

## Scale use and where the panel is informative

Ratings were concentrated in the low categories, and the mean information per rating peaked above the average action. One possible reading is that most match actions are routine and that the panel discriminates best among the more creative actions [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; speculative]. If so, the present panel would be better suited to identifying creative actions than to differentiating among routine ones [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; speculative]. The descriptive pairing of lower leniency with information peaks at higher $\theta$ is consistent with this reading, because less lenient raters reserve their higher categories for more creative actions [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; speculative].

## Contribution and implications

To our knowledge, we have provided the first JRT analysis of CAT ratings of sport actions, based on a large, sparse, but fully connected design of 22 raters, 3,669 football actions, and 7,844 ratings [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. We have shown that judges of football actions differ in leniency and discrimination, that constraining all judges to equal discrimination worsens out-of-sample prediction, and how marginal reliability depends on the number of judges per action [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

Why raters differ in discrimination cannot be answered with the present data, because no rater characteristics were analysed. Several hypotheses are plausible [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. Expertise may act as a continuum rather than a dichotomy, with more experienced judges discriminating more sharply [@kaufman2009; @kaufman2013; @plucker2009] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. Rater characteristics and motivation predict discernment among novice creativity raters [@ceh2022], and workload and fatigue can affect the quality of ratings [@forthmann2017; @ling2014] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. Finally, judges may differ in how they understood the instructions or the definition of creativity [@myszkowski2021] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. Testing these hypotheses requires the rater information requested in the Raters section.

For sport-science researchers, the present study offers a reproducible template: collect CAT ratings in a connected sparse design, score them with JRT, examine whether judges are equally discriminating, and plan the panel size from a D-study [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. Five practical recommendations follow [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]:

1. Use a connected design with sufficient overlap for every rater, because rater parameters depend on the linking set [@wind2018; @wind2019a]. In the present data, the raters with the least overlap also had the least precise parameters [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].
2. When raters rate different subsets of actions, score the ratings with JRT, or at least with a model that includes rater leniency, rather than with raw means [@primi2019; @myszkowski2019] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].
3. Plan the number of judges per action from a D-study or a pilot rather than from a fixed rule [@forthmann2023], and use planned-missing designs to manage rater workload [@primi2019; @forthmann2023] [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].
4. Use discrimination estimates for rater feedback, screening, or calibration [@storme2014; @dollinger2005; @weigle1998], weighing this against the CAT's principle of judgements without imposed criteria [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].
5. Take score precision into account whenever action scores are used downstream, for example as outcome variables or as labels for automated rating; this recommendation is our own argument and is not based on a published source [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

## Limitations and future work

Several limitations should be noted, each of which points to a concrete next step. First, the scope of the study is narrower than the questions that motivated it. Rater expertise, choices concerning the rating scale (number of categories and labels), and comparisons of rating-processing techniques such as mean scores, the MFRM, and generalizability theory were not examined. Future work should compare coaches, players, and lay raters with JRT discrimination as the outcome [@kaufman2013; @zamparo2017], vary the rating scale, and compare scoring approaches on the same data.

Second, the model used thresholds shared by all raters, so response styles beyond leniency were not modelled and the shared category structure was not tested. A JRT graded response or generalized partial credit model with rater-specific thresholds [@myszkowski2021] would allow such a test, but it requires more ratings per rater.

Third, the design was sparse, with about two ratings per action, and three raters (R20 to R22) contributed few ratings, had wide intervals, and shared little overlap with other raters. A benchmark set of actions rated by all judges would strengthen the linking between raters [@wind2019a].

Fourth, actions were not allocated to raters at random with respect to action type, which threatens the assumption that the missing ratings are ignorable. Future studies should randomise the allocation of actions to raters.

Fifth, rater drift was examined only descriptively (Appendix B). Among the 20 raters with at least ten ratings, 3 showed an absolute Spearman correlation greater than .2 between their ratings and the order in which they rated (R01: −.300; R09: −.368; R12: .202); no inference was attached to these values. Future work could add a time facet and use frameworks for monitoring rater drift [@myford2009; @leckie2011; @barth2020], test for differential rater functioning [@wind2019b], or apply the hierarchical rater model [@patz2002] or a generalised MFRM [@uto2020] to multi-facet designs.

Sixth, several computational aspects call for caution. Pareto-$k$ warnings occurred for both models, and only the share of affected observations is available; the effective numbers of parameters were large; the information functions are plug-in values; neither the reliabilities nor the D-study values carry uncertainty; no prior-sensitivity analysis was conducted; and the posterior predictive check was limited to category shares and rater means. Future analyses should apply moment matching or *k*-fold cross-validation and propagate posterior uncertainty into the reliability estimates.

Seventh, only one rating dimension was analysed, and no external criterion was available. The technical-correctness and aesthetic-appeal ratings that were collected could support analyses of discriminant validity [@amabile1982; @zamparo2017], and criteria such as the temporal proximity of actions to goals [@kempe2018] could support analyses of criterion validity.

Finally, the study covers one sport, one pool of actions, and one sample of raters, so the specific parameter values may not generalise. The analysis pipeline, however, is fully reproducible and can be applied directly to other sports, action pools, and rater samples [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM].

# Conclusion

Judges of creative football actions differed in leniency and discrimination, and constraining them to equal discrimination predicted their ratings less well than allowing rater-specific discrimination. At the realised panel size of about two judges per action, the JRT scores reached only modest reliability, and the D-study showed reliability rising with more judges per action. CAT studies in sport should therefore model judges rather than average them, and should plan the number of judges per action empirically [AUTHOR TO CONFIRM]. Future work should examine how rater expertise relates to judge discrimination, test rater-specific thresholds, and compare scoring approaches on the same data.
